habitat: Brackish and saline waters, saltpans, sewage ponds, coastal lagoons and tidal mudflats, more than fresh inland pans.
summary: A small, very pale duck with a pink upturned bill and a uniform head. At a distance it can look almost white. In flight the speculum is mostly white with a dark green centre. The sexes are similar. Immatures resemble adults, and young birds lack the pink on the bill. Newman says it is usually silent. Wikipedia describes a clear whistle from the breeding male and a feeble quack from the female.

similar.note: Red-billed Teal also has a reddish bill, but it has a dark cap, a pale face and a spotted body. Cape Teal is paler and the head is uniform.

sources.title: The Atlas of Southern African Birds, Vol. 1 (Cape Teal)

population.notes: No sourced Kruger estimate is currently available; taxonomy or later records require separate research.

head.pattern: SABAP1 says the head pattern is uniform. Newman says the bird looks almost white at a distance. Wikipedia says the back is browner and the sexes are similar.

wings.pattern: Newman: a predominantly white speculum with a dark green central patch.

viewNotes.note: A small pale duck with a pink upturned bill and no dark cap.
The uniform pale head and pink bill are the front view. There is no dark crown.
The back is browner than the pale body. The speculum is a flight mark.
The speculum is mostly white with a dark green centre.
The underwing is not given a separate colour in these texts.
Wikipedia says young birds lack the pink on the bill. Newman says the immature otherwise resembles the adult. The replacement bill colour is not named.

calls.description: Wikipedia says the breeding male has a clear whistle. Newman says the species is usually silent.
Wikipedia says the female has a feeble quack.

Newman says the species is usually silent. The catalogue cut is not labelled male or female. Grade B, South Africa. A grade A file whose name ends in Cteal-cf was skipped because the cf marks an uncertain identification.

research.note: Months in Kruger are not listed. SABAP1 places it mainly in drier pans and calls it an uncommon visitor to Swaziland and a rare vagrant to southern Mozambique, while the models show no clear migration. Newman treats it as a resident of brackish water. Chick down and the underwing are not described. The call is grade B from the Eastern Cape. The only higher grade in the catalogue had an uncertain cf filename.
